Grandiose

GRAN-dee-ohss -- from Latin grandis, 'big, great,' plus -ose, 'full of': full of grandness, and then some. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Grandiose is excessively grand or ambitious.

The developer's grandiose vision called for a ski slope in the middle of the desert.

Worked Example

A first-year club president announces that the chess team, which has four members and one battered board, will host an international tournament with a live orchestra by December.

A plan far grander than the situation could possibly support is exactly what grandiose describes. Unlike 'ambitious,' which can be admirable, grandiose hints that the whole thing is too big and too showy to be real.

How Grandiose Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

ambitious

ambitious: aiming at something big and difficult

pompous

pompous: self-important and puffed up

showy

showy: designed to attract attention

Antonyms

modest

modest: limited in size or claim

humble

humble: not proud or boastful

How Strong Is It? — ambitious → pompous → grandiose

ambitious vs. grandiose

ambitious vs. grandiose: Ambitious is the neutral, often admiring version of grandiose -- an ambitious plan is merely bold, while a grandiose plan is so oversized that people start to doubt it.

pompous vs. grandiose

pompous vs. grandiose: Pompous is grandiose turned on a person: a grandiose scheme is too grand for reality, while a pompous speaker is too grand in his own opinion of himself.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — grand-

root — grand-: big, great, full-grown (Latin (grandis))

suffix — -ose

suffix — -ose: full of, characterized by (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: Italian grandioso and French grandiose both built on Latin grandis, 'great,' with the ending -osus, 'full of' -- something grandiose is literally 'full of grandness,' the same root behind grand and grandeur.

Use the root in a new word: grandeur

Use the root in a new word: grandeur: Nothing in the photographs prepared them for the grandeur of the canyon at sunrise.

Root Check

Word Choice

Grandiose is nearly always critical. Calling a plan 'grand' praises it; calling it 'grandiose' says it is puffed up beyond what the situation deserves or the planner can deliver.
